arXiv:1507.04582v4 [math.AG] 06 Sep 2016

On rational fixed points of finite group actions on the affine space

Olivier Haution Email address: olivier.haution at gmail.com Address: Mathematisches Institut, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 39, D-80333 München, Germany
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

Consider a finite ll-group acting on the affine space of dimension nn over a field kk, whose characteristic differs from ll. We prove the existence of a fixed point, rational over kk, in the following cases:

— The field kk is pp-special for some prime pp different from its characteristic.

— The field kk is perfect and fertile, and n=3n=3.

1. Introduction

The following question was popularised by Serre in [Ser09].

Let kk be a field, and ll a prime number different from its characteristic. Let GG be a finite ll-group acting by kk-automorphisms on the affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}. Does the action fix a kk-rational point?

The structure of the automorphism group of the affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} over a field (the affine Cremona group) is quite mysterious when n≥3n\geq 3, see e.g. [Kra96]. The question above may be seen as an attempt to provide a small piece of information on this group. Of course the techniques developed to answer this question are likely to be useful to find fixed points for actions on other varieties, but the variety 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} is a particularly interesting test case. The fact that it is not projective prevents the use of many intersection-theoretic techniques. At the same time, one can still hope to answer the question by exploiting the simplicity of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} from a cohomological point of view (its “acyclicity”).

Serre mentions that the answer to his question is unknown when G=ℤ/2G=\mathbb{Z}/2, k=ℚk=\mathbb{Q} and n=3n=3, but gives a positive answer in the two cases listed below.

  • —

    kk is finite.

  • —

    kk is algebraically closed.

He also proves the existence of a fixed point when kk is algebraically closed and GG is instead cyclic of order prime to the characteristic exponent of kk.

Esnault and Nicaise extend in [EN11] the list of fields kk for which the question has a positive answer as follows.

  • —

    kk is separably closed.

  • —

    k=ℝk=\mathbb{R}.

  • —

    kk is a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic zero with algebraically closed residue field of characteristic unequal to ll.

  • —

    kk is a henselian discretely valued field of characteristic zero with residue field finite of cardinality qq, and such that l−1|ql-1\mid q.

They also settle the question when

  • —

    kk is arbitrary and n≤2n\leq 2.

In fact, they prove much more in this case: if GG is a solvable group of order prime to char⁡k\carac k, which acts on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} with n≤2n\leq 2, then (𝔸n)G∈{𝔸0,𝔸1,𝔸2}(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G}\in\{\mathbb{A}^{0},\mathbb{A}^{1},\mathbb{A}^{2}\}.

In the present paper we further extend the list to the following cases.

  • —

    kk is pseudo algebraically closed.

  • —

    kk is qq-special for a prime number q≠char⁡kq\neq\carac k.

  • —

    kk is perfect and fertile, and n=3n=3.

The definitions of “qq-special” and “fertile” will be given below; a field is called pseudo algebraically closed if every geometrically integral variety has a rational point. In this case, the existence of fixed points follows at once from Smith’s theory (see Proposition 3.2.1), and will not be further discussed.

In fact, we answer the analog of Serre’s question where the existence of a rational point is replaced by that of a zero-cycle of degree one (at least over fields of characteristic zero). More precisely, we prove:

Theorem 1.1.

Let kk be a field of characteristic exponent pp. Let GG be a finite group acting on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}. Assume that one of the following assumptions holds.

  1. (i)

    GG is cyclic of order prime to pp.

  2. (ii)

    GG is an ll-group, with l≠pl\neq p.

Then the fixed locus (𝔸n)G(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G} supports a zero-cycle whose degree is a power of pp. If kk is perfect and n≤4n\leq 4, then (𝔸n)G(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G} supports a zero-cycle of degree one.

The proof is based on Hironaka’s resolution of singularities in characteristic zero (and recent results of Cossart-Piltant for threefolds in arbitrary characteristic), on Gabber’s theorem on alterations, and on results of K. Kato and T. Saito concerning wild ramification.

Let qq be a prime number. A field kk is qq-special if the degree of every finite extension of kk is a power of qq. Over such a field, the presence of a zero-cycle of degree prime to qq on a variety is equivalent to that of a rational point. Thus we obtain a positive answer to the original question when kk is a qq-special field with q≠char⁡kq\neq\carac k.

A related question concerns the existence of non-trivial separable forms of the affine space: if XX is kk-variety such that XL≃𝔸LnX_{L}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{n}_{L} for some algebraic separable field extension L/kL/k, do we have X≃𝔸knX\simeq\mathbb{A}^{n}_{k}? It is easy to see that the answer is positive when n∈{0,1}n\in\{0,1\}. This is also the case when n=2n=2 by a result of Shafarevich (see [Sha66], [GD75, (5.8.1)], [Kam75]), but again, very little is known as soon as n≥3n\geq 3, even for k=ℝk=\mathbb{R} and L=ℂL=\mathbb{C} (see [Kra96, Remark 4]). The arguments of the proof of Theorem 1.1 allow us to show (in §3.5) that XX at least supports a zero-cycle whose degree is a power of the characteristic exponent of kk.

The second result of this paper concerns the case n=3n=3 in the question of Serre:

Theorem 1.2.

Let GG be a finite ll-group acting on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} over a perfect field kk, whose characteristic differs from ll. Then the action fixes a k⁡((t))k(\!(t)\!)-rational point.

The conclusion of Theorem 1.2 may be reformulated by saying that any compactification of (𝔸3)G(\mathbb{A}^{3})^{G} has a kk-rational point. A field is called fertile if any dense open subvariety of a smooth variety with a rational point has itself a rational point. This notion was introduced by Pop in [Pop96] (he calls such fields “large fields”); the terminology “fertile” is due to Moret-Bailly. Any finite extension of a fertile field is fertile, and every henselian field is fertile (more examples and references may be found e.g. in [Pop14]). Thus we obtain a positive answer to the question of Serre when kk is perfect and fertile, and n=3n=3.

The notation and conventions used in the paper are given in §2. Theorem 1.1 is proved in §3, and Theorem 1.2 in §4 and §5.

Acknowledgement: I thank Jean-Louis Colliot-Thélène for his remarks. I thank Mathieu Florence and Philippe Gille for pointing out the applications to separable forms of the affine space. I thank Johannes Nicaise whose suggestions led to considerable simplifications in the proof of Theorem 1.2.

2. Notation

In the whole paper, we work over a base field kk, and fix a prime number ll unequal to its characteristic.

2.1. Varieties

We denote by ks{{k}_{s}} a separable algebraic closure of kk. A variety, or kk-variety, is a reduced separated scheme of finite type over kk. Closed subsets of a variety will be considered as closed subvarieties using the reduced structure. If L/kL/k is a field extension and XX a kk-variety, we will write XLX_{L} for the LL-variety obtained by extending scalars and taking the underlying reduced scheme. We will say that a variety XX is geometrically irreducible, resp. connected, if XksX_{{k}_{s}} is irreducible, resp. connected (the empty set is neither connected nor irreducible). The residue field of a point xx of XX will be denoted by κ⁡(x)\kappa(x). A variety is complete if it is proper over kk. A variety is a compactification of XX if it is complete and contains XX as a dense open subscheme; a compactification always exists by a theorem of Nagata [Lüt93].

The index nXn_{X} of a variety XX is the g.c.d. of the degrees of its closed points (it is zero when X=∅X=\varnothing).

The subset Sing⁡(X)\Sing(X) of points x∈Xx\in X such that the local ring 𝒪X,x\mathcal{O}_{X,x} is not regular is closed in XX by a theorem of Zariski [Gro65, (6.12.5)]. The variety XX is regular when Sing⁡(X)=∅\Sing(X)=\varnothing.

When XX is a smooth variety, we denote by TXT_{X} its tangent bundle.

We denote by 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} the kk-variety Spec⁡k⁡[t1,⋯,tn]\Spec k[t_{1},\cdots,t_{n}].

2.2. Normal crossing divisors

An effective Cartier divisor D→XD\to X will be called a snc divisor if for every x∈Xx\in X there is a regular system of parameters f1,⋯,fnf_{1},\cdots,f_{n} in 𝒪X,x\mathcal{O}_{X,x} such that the ideal 𝒪​(−D)x\mathcal{O}(-D)_{x} of 𝒪X,x\mathcal{O}_{X,x} is generated by the element (f1)r1⋯(fn)rn(f_{1})^{r_{1}}\cdots(f_{n})^{r_{n}} for some integers ri≥0r_{i}\geq 0 (see [Liu02, Definition 9.1.6]). We will say that a closed subvariety of XX is the support of a snc divisor in XX if it underlies some snc divisor.

If YY is the support of a snc divisor in XX, then XX is regular. One also sees easily that each irreducible component of YY is regular, and that no point of codimension nn in XX belongs to more than nn irreducible components of YY.

Lemma 2.2.1.

Let XX be a kk-variety, and L/kL/k a separable algebraic field extension. If YY is the support of a snc divisor in XX, then so is YLY_{L} in XLX_{L}.

Proof.

It will suffice to prove that if D→XD\to X is a snc divisor, then so is DL→XLD_{L}\to X_{L}. Let y∈XLy\in X_{L} and x∈Xx\in X its image. Write A=𝒪X,xA=\mathcal{O}_{X,x} and B=𝒪XL,yB=\mathcal{O}_{X_{L},y}. Let f1,⋯,fnf_{1},\cdots,f_{n} be a regular system of parameters in AA such that the ideal 𝒪X​(−D)x\mathcal{O}_{X}(-D)_{x} of AA is generated by the element (f1)r1⋯(fn)rn(f_{1})^{r_{1}}\cdots(f_{n})^{r_{n}}. Then the ideal 𝒪XL​(−DL)y\mathcal{O}_{X_{L}}(-D_{L})_{y} of BB is generated by the image of this element. It will therefore suffice to prove that (the images of) f1,⋯,fnf_{1},\cdots,f_{n} form a regular system of parameters in BB. Let C=A⊗kLC=A\otimes_{k}L. The noetherian ring κ⁡(x)⊗kL=C/(f1,⋯,fn)\kappa(x)\otimes_{k}L=C/(f_{1},\cdots,f_{n}) is integral over κ⁡(x)\kappa(x) (because L/kL/k is algebraic) and reduced (because L/kL/k is separable). Therefore the ring C/(f1,⋯,fn)C/(f_{1},\cdots,f_{n}) is reduced and artinian, and so is its localisation B/(f1,⋯,fn)B/(f_{1},\cdots,f_{n}). The latter is additionally local, hence must be a field, showing that f1,⋯,fnf_{1},\cdots,f_{n} generate the maximal ideal of BB. This concludes the proof, since dimB=dimA=n\dim B=\dim A=n by [Gro65, (6.1.3)] applied to the morphism A→BA\to B. ∎

2.3. Group actions

When GG is a finite group, an action of GG on a variety XX will mean an action by kk-automorphisms. The fixed locus XGX^{G} is a closed subvariety of XX such that XG​(L)=X​(L)GX^{G}(L)=X(L)^{G} for any field extension L/kL/k. In fact, there is a scheme-theoretic version of the fixed locus, defined as the intersection in XX of the equalisers of idX\id_{X} and the action of σ\sigma, where σ\sigma runs over GG. The variety XGX^{G} is the underlying reduced scheme. When XX is smooth and the order of GG is prime to the characteristic of kk, then the scheme-theoretic fixed locus is smooth [Edi92, Proposition 3.4], hence coincides with the variety XGX^{G}.

2.4. Cohomology groups

Let XX be a variety. We will write Hi​(Xks,ℚl)H^{i}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}) (resp. Hci​(Xks,ℚl)H^{i}_{c}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})) for the étale cohomology groups (resp. with compact supports) with ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}-coefficients of the ks{{k}_{s}}-variety XksX_{{k}_{s}}.

2.5. Graphs

By a graph, we will mean be a finite undirected graph. In other words, a graph Γ\Gamma consists in a finite set of vertices V⁡(Γ)V(\Gamma), and for each unordered pair of vertices {v1,v2}\{v_{1},v_{2}\} a finite set of edges E⁡({v1,v2})E(\{v_{1},v_{2}\}). If e∈E⁡({v1,v2})e\in E(\{v_{1},v_{2}\}) we say that v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} are the extremities of the edge ee, or that ee is an edge between v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}. Declaring two vertices equivalent if there is an edge between them generates an equivalence relation on V⁡(Γ)V(\Gamma). The graph Γ\Gamma will be called connected if there is exactly one equivalence class. A tree is a connected graph with n−1n-1 edges and nn vertices, for some n≥1n\geq 1. A vertex vv of a tree is called a leaf if there is at most one edge one of whose extremities is vv.

3. Zero-cycles of degree one

3.1. Euler characteristic and index

Definition 3.1.1.

The Euler characteristic (with compact supports) of a variety XX is defined as:

χ⁡(X)=∑i(−1)i​dimℚlHci​(Xks,ℚl).\chi(X)=\sum_{i}(-1)^{i}\dim_{{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}}H^{i}_{c}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}).

If ZZ is a closed subvariety of XX, then the long exact sequence of cohomology groups with compact supports [Mil80, III, Remark 1.30] yields the relation

χ⁡(X)=χ⁡(Z)+χ⁡(X−Z).\chi(X)=\chi(Z)+\chi(X-Z).

In the next proposition, we denote by cc the total Chern class with values in the Chow group.

Proposition 3.1.2.

Let XX be a smooth complete variety. Then χ⁡(X)=deg⁡c⁡(TX)\chi(X)=\deg c(T_{X}). In particular XX supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(X)\chi(X).

Proof.

This follows from the Lefschetz trace formula [Mil80, VI, Theorem 12.3] and the self-intersection formula [Ful98, Example 8.1.12]. ∎

Lemma 3.1.3.

Let L/kL/k be a purely inseparable field extension, and XX a non-empty kk-variety. Then nX/nXLn_{X}/n_{X_{L}} is a power of the characteristic exponent of kk.

Proof.

Let pp be the characteristic exponent of kk. Let xx be a closed point of XLX_{L}. Its image yy in XX is a closed point, because the extension L/kL/k is algebraic. By multiplicativity of separable degrees [Lan02, V, Theorem 4.1], we have in ℕ∪{∞}\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}

[κ(x):L]s⋅[L:k]s=[κ(x):k]s=[κ(x):κ(y)]s⋅[κ(y):k]s.[\kappa(x):L]_{s}\cdot[L:k]_{s}=[\kappa(x):k]_{s}=[\kappa(x):\kappa(y)]_{s}\cdot[\kappa(y):k]_{s}.

By assumption we have [L:k]s=1[L:k]_{s}=1, and since the extension κ⁡(x)/L\kappa(x)/L is finite, all the above displayed separable degrees are finite. It follows that

[κ(y):k]s∣[κ(x):L]s.[\kappa(y):k]_{s}\mid[\kappa(x):L]_{s}.

Since the extension κ⁡(y)/k\kappa(y)/k is finite, there is an integer mm such that [κ(y):k]=pm⋅[κ(y):k]s[\kappa(y):k]=p^{m}\cdot[\kappa(y):k]_{s}. Thus we have a chain of divisibilities

nX∣[κ(y):k]∣pm⋅[κ(x):L]s∣pm⋅[κ(x):L].n_{X}\mid[\kappa(y):k]\mid p^{m}\cdot[\kappa(x):L]_{s}\mid p^{m}\cdot[\kappa(x):L].

Let now x1,⋯,xn∈XLx_{1},\cdots,x_{n}\in X_{L} be a finite family of closed points such that nXLn_{X_{L}} is the g.c.d. of [κ(x1):L],⋯,[κ(xn):L][\kappa(x_{1}):L],\cdots,[\kappa(x_{n}):L]. As we have just seen, we may find for each ii an integer mim_{i} such that nX∣pmi⋅[κ(xi):L]n_{X}\mid p^{m_{i}}\cdot[\kappa(x_{i}):L]. Letting mm be the maximum of the mim_{i}’s, we obtain that nX|pm⋅nXLn_{X}\mid p^{m}\cdot n_{X_{L}}.

On the other hand any zero-cycle on XX gives rise by scalars extension to a zero-cycle of the same degree on the LL-scheme X⊗kLX\otimes_{k}L, and therefore also on the underlying LL-variety XLX_{L}. Thus nXL|nXn_{X_{L}}\mid n_{X}, and the statement follows. ∎

Proposition 3.1.4.

Let XX be a kk-variety.

  1. (i)

    If char⁡k=0\carac k=0, or if kk is perfect and dimX≤3\dim X\leq 3, then XX supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(X)\chi(X).

  2. (ii)

    If char⁡k=p>0\carac k=p>0, then XX supports a zero-cycle of degree pm⋅χ⁡(X)p^{m}\cdot\chi(X), for some integer mm.

Proof.

(i): We proceed by induction on dimX\dim X; if X=∅X=\varnothing, then χ⁡(X)=0\chi(X)=0 and XX supports the null zero-cycle. While proving the statement, one may replace XX by any dense open subvariety. Indeed assume that such a subvariety UU of XX supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(U)\chi(U). Then so does XX. Since by induction X−UX-U supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(X−U)\chi(X-U), so does again XX. Therefore XX supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(X)=χ⁡(U)+χ⁡(U−X)\chi(X)=\chi(U)+\chi(U-X).

In particular we may replace XX by a smooth dense open subvariety (which exists since kk is perfect). Then we may find a smooth compactification X′X^{\prime} of XX; this result is due to Hironaka [Hir64] when char⁡k=0\carac k=0, to Abhyankar (see e.g. Lipman’s [Lip78]) when dimX≤2\dim X\leq 2, and to Cossart and Piltant [CP14] when dimX≤3\dim X\leq 3. Then X′X^{\prime} supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(X′)\chi(X^{\prime}) by Proposition 3.1.2, and by induction Z=X′−XZ=X^{\prime}-X (hence also X′X^{\prime}) supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(Z)\chi(Z). It follows that X′X^{\prime} supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(X′)−χ⁡(Z)=χ⁡(X)\chi(X^{\prime})-\chi(Z)=\chi(X). The same is true for its dense open subvariety XX, by a moving lemma [GLL13, Proposition 6.8] (see also [CT05, p.599]).

(ii): We let qq be a prime number different from pp and denote by vqv_{q} the qq-adic valuation on ℤ\mathbb{Z}. We need to prove that vq​(nX)≤vq​(χ⁡(X))v_{q}(n_{X})\leq v_{q}(\chi(X)). Replacing kk by a perfect closure affects neither χ⁡(X)\chi(X) [SGA72, VIII, Théorème 1.1] nor vq​(nX)v_{q}(n_{X}) (Lemma 3.1.3). Thus we may assume that kk is perfect. We again proceed by induction on dimX\dim X. Induction on the number of irreducible components of XX shows that we may assume that XX is irreducible (the argument is the same as beginning of the proof of (i)). Let X′X^{\prime} be a compactification of XX. By the results of Gabber on alterations [ILO, Introduction, Theorem 3 (1), or X, Theorem 3.5 (iii)], we may find a smooth complete variety Y′Y^{\prime}, a morphism f:Y′→X′f\colon Y^{\prime}\to X^{\prime}, a non-empty open subvariety UU of X′X^{\prime} such that V=f−1​UV=f^{-1}U is dense in Y′Y^{\prime} and V→UV\to U is étale and finite of degree dd, with dd prime to qq. Shrinking UU, we may assume that UU is smooth and contained in XX. It will suffice to prove that vq​(nU)≤vq​(χ⁡(U))v_{q}(n_{U})\leq v_{q}(\chi(U)) (see the argument at the beginning of the proof of (i)). Consider the variety B=X′−UB=X^{\prime}-U (with reduced structure). Let X′′X^{\prime\prime} be the blow-up of BB in X′X^{\prime}, and Y′′Y^{\prime\prime} the blow-up of the (possibly non-reduced) closed subscheme f−1​Bf^{-1}B of Y′Y^{\prime}. There is an induced morphism Y′′→X′′Y^{\prime\prime}\to X^{\prime\prime}. Using once again the result of Gabber, we find a smooth complete variety Z′′Z^{\prime\prime}, a morphism g:Z′′→Y′′g\colon Z^{\prime\prime}\to Y^{\prime\prime} generically of degree prime to qq and such that W=g−1​VW=g^{-1}V is the complement of a snc divisor in Z′′Z^{\prime\prime}. We now use results of K. Kato et T. Saito. We have by [KS08, Lemma 3.4.5.1]

(1) deg⁡DV/Ul​o​g=d⋅χ⁡(U)−χ⁡(V)∈ℚ,\deg D^{log}_{V/U}=d\cdot\chi(U)-\chi(V)\in\mathbb{Q},

where DV/Ul​o​g∈CH0⁡(V¯\V)⊗ℤℚD^{log}_{V/U}\in\CH_{0}(\overline{V}\backslash V)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q} is the wild different [KS08, Definition 3.4.1], and CH0⁡(V¯\V)\CH_{0}(\overline{V}\backslash V) is the Chow group of zero-cycles on the boundary [KS08, Definition 3.1.1]. We apply [KS08, Theorem 3.2.3.1], where the diagram (3.4) of [KS08] is

and obtain that the image of DV/Ul​o​gD^{log}_{V/U} under the natural morphism CH0⁡(V¯\V)⊗ℤℚ→CH0⁡(Y′′−V)⊗ℤℚ\CH_{0}(\overline{V}\backslash V)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}\to\CH_{0}(Y^{\prime\prime}-V)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q} lies in the image of the morphism CH0⁡(Y′′−V)⊗ℤℤ(q)→CH0⁡(Y′′−V)⊗ℤℚ\CH_{0}(Y^{\prime\prime}-V)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}_{(q)}\to\CH_{0}(Y^{\prime\prime}-V)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q} (here ℤ(q)⊂ℚ\mathbb{Z}_{(q)}\subset\mathbb{Q} denotes those fractions whose denominator is prime to qq). Since there is a morphism Y′′−V→Y′Y^{\prime\prime}-V\to Y^{\prime}, we deduce that

(2) vq​(nY′)≤vq​(nY′′−V)≤vq​(deg⁡DV/Ul​o​g).v_{q}(n_{Y^{\prime}})\leq v_{q}(n_{Y^{\prime\prime}-V})\leq v_{q}(\deg D^{log}_{V/U}).

On the other hand vq​(nY′)≤vq​(χ⁡(Y′))v_{q}(n_{Y^{\prime}})\leq v_{q}(\chi(Y^{\prime})) (by Proposition 3.1.2, since Y′Y^{\prime} is smooth), and by induction vq​(nY′−V)≤vq​(χ⁡(Y′−V))v_{q}(n_{Y^{\prime}-V})\leq v_{q}(\chi(Y^{\prime}-V)). Using the relation nY′|nY′−Vn_{Y^{\prime}}\mid n_{Y^{\prime}-V}, we obtain

(3) vq​(nY′)≤vq​(χ⁡(Y′)−χ⁡(Y′−V))=vq​(χ⁡(V)).v_{q}(n_{Y^{\prime}})\leq v_{q}(\chi(Y^{\prime})-\chi(Y^{\prime}-V))=v_{q}(\chi(V)).

Combining (1), (2), (3), we deduce that vq​(nY′)≤vq​(χ⁡(U))v_{q}(n_{Y^{\prime}})\leq v_{q}(\chi(U)). Finally nY′=nVn_{Y^{\prime}}=n_{V} (by the moving lemma [GLL13, Proposition 6.8], since VV is dense in the smooth variety Y′Y^{\prime}), and nU|nVn_{U}\mid n_{V} (since there is a morphism V→UV\to U). We conclude that vq​(nU)≤vq​(χ⁡(U))v_{q}(n_{U})\leq v_{q}(\chi(U)), as required. ∎

Remark 3.1.5.

Statement (i) could be improved (by removing the assumption dimX≤3\dim X\leq 3, for kk perfect) if we could resolve singularities in positive characteristic. On the other hand, we may see that (ii) is optimal by considering the case when XX is the spectrum of a finite purely inseparable field extension of kk.

3.2. Actions of ll-groups on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}

Proposition 3.2.1.

Let ll be a prime number unequal to char⁡k\carac k. Let GG be a finite ll-group acting on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} over kk, and S=(𝔸n)GS=(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G}. Then SS is smooth, geometrically connected, and satisfies χ⁡(S)=1\chi(S)=1. More precisely:

Hi​(Sks,ℚl)={0 if i≠0ℚl if i=0, and ​Hci​(Sks,ℚl)={0 if i≠2​dimSℚl if i=2​dimS.H^{i}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0&\mbox{ if $i\neq 0$}\\ {\mathbb{Q}_{l}}&\mbox{ if $i=0$}\end{array},\right.\text{ and }\;H^{i}_{c}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0&\mbox{ if $i\neq 2\dim S$}\\ {\mathbb{Q}_{l}}&\mbox{ if $i=2\dim S$}\end{array}.\right.
Proof.

The variety SS is smooth (see §2.3), and by Poincaré duality it will suffice to prove the statements concerning Hi​(Sks,ℚl)H^{i}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}). Replacing kk by a perfect closure do not affect Hi​(Sks,ℚl)H^{i}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}) by [SGA72, VIII, Théorème 1.1], so that we may assume that kk is perfect.

Let us say that a variety XX is AA-acyclic if the étale cohomology groups with coefficients in AA satisfy Hét0​(Xks,A)=AH^{0}_{\text{\'{e}t}}(X_{{{k}_{s}}},A)=A and Héti​(Xks,A)=0H^{i}_{\text{\'{e}t}}(X_{{{k}_{s}}},A)=0 for i≠0i\neq 0. The variety 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} is ℤ/l\mathbb{Z}/l-acyclic [Mil80, Corollary 4.20], and it follows from Smith’s theory [Ser09, Theorem 7.5 and its corollary] that SS is also ℤ/l\mathbb{Z}/l-acyclic. Using the exact sequence

0→ℤ/lm→ℤ/lm+1→ℤ/l→00\to\mathbb{Z}/l^{m}\to\mathbb{Z}/l^{m+1}\to\mathbb{Z}/l\to 0

we see by induction on mm that SS is ℤ/lm\mathbb{Z}/l^{m}-acyclic for every positive integer mm. Taking the limit over mm, it follows that SS is ℤl\mathbb{Z}_{l}-acyclic, and tensoring with ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}} over ℤl\mathbb{Z}_{l}, we conclude that SS is ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}-acyclic. ∎

Theorem 3.2.2.

Let kk be a field of characteristic exponent pp, and ll a prime number unequal to pp. Let GG be a finite ll-group acting on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} over kk. Then (𝔸n)G(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G} supports a zero-cycle whose degree is a power of pp. If kk is perfect and n≤4n\leq 4, then (𝔸n)G(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G} supports a zero-cycle of degree one.

Proof.

Since χ⁡((𝔸n)G)=1\chi((\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G})=1 by Proposition 3.2.1, the statement follows from Proposition 3.1.4 (we may assume that GG acts non-trivially, so that dim(𝔸n)G≤3\dim(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G}\leq 3 when n≤4n\leq 4). ∎

3.3. Actions of cyclic groups on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}

Theorem 3.3.1.

Let kk be a field of characteristic exponent pp. Let GG be a finite cyclic group of order prime to pp acting on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} over kk. Then (𝔸n)G(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G} supports a zero-cycle whose degree is a power of pp. If kk is perfect and n≤4n\leq 4, then (𝔸n)G(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G} supports a zero-cycle of degree one.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.1.3 we may assume that kk is perfect. Let gg be a generator of GG. By a result of Deligne-Lusztig [DL76, Theorem 3.2] we have

(4) ∑i(−1)i​Tr⁡(g∗:Hci​(𝔸ksn,ℚl))=χ⁡((𝔸n)G).\sum_{i}(-1)^{i}\Tr\big(g^{*}:H^{i}_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{n}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\big)=\chi\big((\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G}\big).

Using [Mil80, Corollary 4.20] for F=ℤ/lmF=\mathbb{Z}/l^{m} and taking the limit over mm and tensoring with ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}} over ℤl\mathbb{Z}_{l}, and using Poincaré duality, we see that Hci​(𝔸ksn,ℚl)=0H^{i}_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{n}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0 if i≠2​ni\neq 2n and Hc2​n​(𝔸ksn,ℚl)=ℚlH^{2n}_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{n}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})={\mathbb{Q}_{l}}. Moreover GG acts trivially on the set of connected components of 𝔸ksn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{{k}_{s}}, and thus also on H0​(𝔸ksn,ℚl)≃Hc2​n​(𝔸ksn,ℚl)H^{0}(\mathbb{A}^{n}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\simeq H^{2n}_{c}(\mathbb{A}^{n}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}). Therefore the value of the left hand side of (4) is 11, and we conclude using Proposition 3.1.4, as in the proof of Theorem 3.2.2. ∎

3.4. qq-special fields

Let qq be a prime number. The field kk is called qq-special if the degree of every finite extension of kk is a power of qq. The combination of Theorem 3.2.2 and Theorem 3.3.1 is Theorem 1.1 of the introduction, and has the following consequence.

Corollary 3.4.1 (of Theorem 1.1).

Let kk be a field of characteristic exponent pp. Assume that kk is qq-special, for some prime number qq unequal to pp. Then the action on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} of any finite ll-group with l≠pl\neq p, or any finite cyclic group of order prime to pp, fixes a kk-rational point.

This corollary applies to real-closed fields, which are 22-special and of characteristic zero. In particular, we obtain a purely algebraic proof for the case k=ℝk=\mathbb{R} (the classical proof uses algebraic topology, see e.g. [EN11, §5.4]).

3.5. Separable forms of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}

As mentioned in the introduction, it is currently unknown whether every ℝ\mathbb{R}-variety XX such that Xℂ≃𝔸ℂnX_{\mathbb{C}}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}} is isomorphic to 𝔸ℝn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{R}} (for n≥3n\geq 3). A consequence of the next proposition is that XX must have an ℝ\mathbb{R}-point.

Proposition 3.5.1.

Let kk be a field of characteristic exponent pp, and XX a kk-variety such that Xks≃𝔸ksnX_{{{k}_{s}}}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{n}_{{{k}_{s}}}. Then XX supports a zero-cycle whose degree is a power of pp. If kk is perfect and n≤3n\leq 3, then XX supports a zero-cycle of degree one. If kk is qq-special for some prime number qq unequal to pp, then X⁡(k)≠∅X(k)\neq\varnothing.

Proof.

This follows from Proposition 3.1.4 and the fact that χ⁡(𝔸n)=1\chi(\mathbb{A}^{n})=1, already observed in the course of the proof of Theorem 3.3.1. ∎

4. Actions of ll-groups on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}

A field FF is called fertile if any dense open subvariety of a smooth FF-variety with an FF-rational point has itself an FF-rational point. When a (smooth) kk-variety SS admits a smooth compactification S′S^{\prime}, the following conditions are equivalent.

  • —

    Every compactification of SS has a kk-rational point.

  • —

    The variety SS has an FF-rational point for any fertile field FF containing kk.

  • —

    The variety SS has a k⁡((t))k(\!(t)\!)-rational point.

Indeed, any of these conditions is equivalent to the condition S′​(k)≠∅S^{\prime}(k)\neq\varnothing (this follows from Nishimura’s Lemma, the valuative criterion of properness and the fact that k⁡((t))k(\!(t)\!) is fertile, see [Pop14, §1.A.2)]).

Theorem 4.1.

Let kk be a perfect field, and ll a prime number different from its characteristic. Let GG be a finite ll-group acting on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} over kk. Then the variety S=(𝔸3)GS=(\mathbb{A}^{3})^{G} satisfies the three above conditions.

Proof.

By Proposition 3.2.1, the variety SS is geometrically connected, smooth and satisfies χ⁡(S)=1\chi(S)=1. If dimS=0\dim S=0, then SS must be a single rational point. If dimS=3\dim S=3, then S=𝔸3S=\mathbb{A}^{3}. In these two cases, the conclusion of the theorem holds.

We now assume that dimS∈{1,2}\dim S\in\{1,2\}. Since kk is perfect, the variety SS admits a smooth compactification S′S^{\prime} such that the closed subvariety D=S′−SD=S^{\prime}-S is the support of a snc divisor in XX (§2.2), by [Lip78] and [Liu02, Theorem 9.2.26]. It will suffice to prove that S′​(k)≠∅S^{\prime}(k)\neq\varnothing. The variety S′S^{\prime} is geometrically connected because its dense open subvariety SS is so. Moreover Hc1​(Sks,ℚl)=0H^{1}_{c}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0 by Proposition 3.2.1. The exact sequence of ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}-vector spaces

H0​(Sks′,ℚl)→H0​(Dks,ℚl)→Hc1​(Sks,ℚl)H^{0}(S^{\prime}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{0}(D_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{1}_{c}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})

then shows that DD is geometrically connected.

In case dimS=1\dim S=1, the variety DD is non-empty because SS is affine. Thus dimD=0\dim D=0, and DD must be a single rational point (kk is perfect), which concludes the proof in this case. But we can say more: the exact sequence of ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}-vector spaces

Hc1​(Sks,ℚl)→H1​(Sks′,ℚl)→H1​(Dks,ℚl)H^{1}_{c}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{1}(S^{\prime}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{1}(D_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})

shows that H1​(Sks′,ℚl)=0H^{1}(S^{\prime}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0. Thus the kk-variety S′S^{\prime} is a smooth complete curve of genus zero (see e.g. [SGA73, IX, §4]), that is, a conic. It has a rational point, hence is isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, and S=ℙ1−D≃𝔸1S=\mathbb{P}^{1}-D\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}.

We now assume that dimS=2\dim S=2. By semi-purity [Mil80, VI, Lemma 9.1], the restriction morphisms Hét1​(Sks′,ℤ/lm)→Hét1​(Sks,ℤ/lm)H^{1}_{\text{\'{e}t}}(S^{\prime}_{{k}_{s}},\mathbb{Z}/l^{m})\to H^{1}_{\text{\'{e}t}}(S_{{k}_{s}},\mathbb{Z}/l^{m}) are injective for all mm, and by left-exactness of the inverse limit and flatness of ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}} over ℤl\mathbb{Z}_{l}, it follows that H1​(Sks′,ℚl)→H1​(Sks,ℚl)H^{1}(S^{\prime}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{1}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}) is injective. Since by Proposition 3.2.1 we have H1​(Sks,ℚl)=0H^{1}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0, we deduce that H1​(Sks′,ℚl)=0H^{1}(S^{\prime}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0. Proposition 3.2.1 also yields Hc2​(Sks,ℚl)=0H^{2}_{c}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0, and the exact sequence of ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}-vector spaces

H1​(Sks′,ℚl)→H1​(Dks,ℚl)→Hc2​(Sks,ℚl)H^{1}(S^{\prime}_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{1}(D_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{2}_{c}(S_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})

shows that H1​(Dks,ℚl)=0H^{1}(D_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0. By Lemma 4.3, the variety DD supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(S)\chi(S), and χ⁡(S)=1\chi(S)=1 by Proposition 3.2.1. We prove in Proposition 5.3.1 below that D⁡(k)≠∅D(k)\neq\varnothing, which implies that S′​(k)≠∅S^{\prime}(k)\neq\varnothing. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Let kk be an arbitrary field, and ll a prime number different from its characteristic. Let GG be a finite ll-group acting on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} over kk, with nn arbitrary. Let S=(𝔸n)GS=(\mathbb{A}^{n})^{G}. The proof of Theorem 4.1 shows the following.

  • —

    If dimS=n\dim S=n, then S=𝔸nS=\mathbb{A}^{n}.

  • —

    If dimS=0\dim S=0, then SS is a single kk-rational point

  • —

    If dimS=1\dim S=1 and kk is perfect, then S≃𝔸1S\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}. In case n=2n=2, this was proved in [EN11, Theorem 5.12] without assuming that kk is perfect.

However, our proof breaks down when dimS=2\dim S=2 and n>3n>3 because Lemma 4.3 below seems to be specific to subvarieties of codimension one in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}.

Lemma 4.3.

Assume that the field kk is perfect. Let SS be a smooth closed subvariety of pure codimension one in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}, with 2≤n≤42\leq n\leq 4. Let S′S^{\prime} be a smooth compactification of SS. Then D=S′−SD=S^{\prime}-S supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(S)\chi(S).

Proof.

The closed embedding i:S→𝔸ni\colon S\to\mathbb{A}^{n} is an effective Cartier divisor; let L=𝒪⁡(S)L=\mathcal{O}(S) be the corresponding line bundle on 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}. Then we have an exact sequence of vector bundles on SS [Gro67, (17.13.2.1)]

0→TS→i∗​T𝔸n→i∗​L→0.0\to T_{S}\to i^{*}T_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}\to i^{*}L\to 0.

Thus [TS]∈K0​(S)[T_{S}]\in K_{0}(S) is in the image of the morphism i∗:K0​(𝔸n)→K0​(S)i^{*}\colon K_{0}(\mathbb{A}^{n})\to K_{0}(S). By homotopy invariance [Qui73, §6, Corollary of Theorem 9], the natural morphism ℤ→K0​(𝔸n)\mathbb{Z}\to K_{0}(\mathbb{A}^{n}) is an isomorphism, and we deduce that [TS]=rank⁡TS=n−1∈K0​(S)[T_{S}]=\rank T_{S}=n-1\in K_{0}(S). This implies that cn−1​(TS)=0∈CH0⁡(S)c_{n-1}(T_{S})=0\in\CH_{0}(S), because the Chern classes of a vector bundle depend only on its class in K0K_{0} [Ful98, Example 3.2.7 (b)], and the (n−1)(n-1)-st Chern class of a trivial bundle vanishes (since n−1>0n-1>0). Now TS=(TS′)|ST_{S}=(T_{S^{\prime}})|_{S}, hence cn−1​(TS′)|S=0∈CH0⁡(S)c_{n-1}(T_{S^{\prime}})|_{S}=0\in\CH_{0}(S). By the localisation sequence for Chow groups [Ful98, Proposition 1.8], it follows that the cycle class cn−1​(TS′)c_{n-1}(T_{S^{\prime}}) lies in the image of the morphism CH0⁡(D)→CH0⁡(S′)\CH_{0}(D)\to\CH_{0}(S^{\prime}). Thus DD supports a zero-cycle of degree deg⁡cn−1​(TS′)\deg c_{n-1}(T_{S^{\prime}}), and deg⁡cn−1​(TS′)=χ⁡(S′)\deg c_{n-1}(T_{S^{\prime}})=\chi(S^{\prime}) by Proposition 3.1.2. Since the variety DD also supports a zero-cycle of degree χ⁡(D)\chi(D) by Proposition 3.1.4 (i) (because n−1≤3n-1\leq 3), it must support one of degree χ⁡(S)=χ⁡(S′)−χ⁡(D)\chi(S)=\chi(S^{\prime})-\chi(D). ∎

5. One-dimensional snc divisors with no H1H^{1}

5.1. The geometric number of components

Definition 5.1.1.

Let XX be a variety. We define mXm_{X}, resp. μX\mu_{X}, as the number of irreducible, resp. connected, components of the ks{{k}_{s}}-variety XksX_{{{k}_{s}}}.

When XX is a variety, we have

(5) μX=dimℚlH0​(Xks,ℚl).\mu_{X}=\dim_{{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}}H^{0}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}).
Lemma 5.1.2.

Let XX be a variety of pure dimension nn. Then

mX=dimℚlHc2​n​(Xks,ℚl).m_{X}=\dim_{{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}}H^{2n}_{c}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}).
Proof.

Replacing kk by a perfect closure affects neither mXm_{X} (this operation does not affect the topological space XksX_{{k}_{s}}) nor Hc2​n​(Xks,ℚl)H^{2n}_{c}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}) [SGA72, VIII, Théorème 1.1]. Thus we may assume that kk is perfect. Let UU be a smooth dense open subvariety of XX, and ZZ its complement. We have an exact sequence of ℚl{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}-vector spaces

Hc2​n−1​(Zks,ℚl)→Hc2​n​(Uks,ℚl)→Hc2​n​(Xks,ℚl)→Hc2​n​(Zks,ℚl),H^{2n-1}_{c}(Z_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{2n}_{c}(U_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{2n}_{c}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})\to H^{2n}_{c}(Z_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}),

where the two extreme groups vanish since dimZ<n\dim Z<n. Using Poincaré duality and (5), we deduce that

dimℚlHc2​n​(Xks,ℚl)=dimℚlHc2​n​(Uks,ℚl)=dimℚlH0​(Uks,ℚl)=μU.\dim_{{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}}H^{2n}_{c}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=\dim_{{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}}H^{2n}_{c}(U_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=\dim_{{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}}H^{0}(U_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=\mu_{U}.

The result follows, since mX=mUm_{X}=m_{U} (the set UksU_{{{k}_{s}}} is dense in the noetherian space XksX_{{{k}_{s}}}), and mU=μUm_{U}=\mu_{U} (the scheme UksU_{{{k}_{s}}} is locally irreducible, being smooth). ∎

Lemma 5.1.3.

Let XX be a connected complete variety. Then μX|nX\mu_{X}\mid n_{X}.

Proof.

When X=Spec⁡FX=\Spec F for a finite field extension F/kF/k, the integer μX\mu_{X} is the separable degree [F:k]s[F:k]_{s}, which divides the degree [F:k]=nX[F:k]=n_{X}.

In general, the kk-algebra F=H0​(X,𝒪X)F=H^{0}(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}) is reduced and finite, and moreover the kk-variety Spec⁡F\Spec F is connected. Thus FF is a finite field extension of kk. Since μSpec⁡F=μX\mu_{\Spec F}=\mu_{X}, and nSpec⁡F|nXn_{\Spec F}\mid n_{X}, we conclude using the special case treated above. ∎

5.2. The dual graph

Definition 5.2.1.

Let XX be a kk-variety. The dual graph of XX, denoted henceforth ΓX\Gamma_{X}, is the undirected graph defined as follows. Its vertices are the irreducible components of of the ks{{k}_{s}}-variety XksX_{{{k}_{s}}} (its cardinality is thus mXm_{X}). The set of edges between two irreducible components is empty if they coincide, and equal to the set of irreducible components (over ks{{k}_{s}}) of their intersection otherwise.

The graph ΓX\Gamma_{X} is naturally endowed with an action of the absolute Galois group Gal⁡(ks/k)\Gal({{k}_{s}}/k), and orbits in the set of vertices correspond bijectively to irreducible components of XX by [Sta15, Tag 04KY].

Lemma 5.2.2.

A variety XX is geometrically connected if and only if its dual graph ΓX\Gamma_{X} is connected.

Proof.

First note that X=∅X=\varnothing if and only if ΓX=∅\Gamma_{X}=\varnothing. Associating to a set of vertices VV the union α⁡(V)\alpha(V) of the corresponding irreducible components yields a bijection between the subsets of V⁡(ΓX)V(\Gamma_{X}) and the subsets of XksX_{{k}_{s}} which are unions of irreducible components of XX. We have α⁡(V1∪V2)=α⁡(V1)∪α⁡(V2)\alpha(V_{1}\cup V_{2})=\alpha(V_{1})\cup\alpha(V_{2}). Moreover α⁡(V1)∩α⁡(V2)=∅\alpha(V_{1})\cap\alpha(V_{2})=\varnothing if and only if V1∩V2=∅V_{1}\cap V_{2}=\varnothing and there are no edges between elements V1V_{1} and V2V_{2}. To conclude the proof, note that a closed and open subset of XksX_{{k}_{s}} is necessarily a union of irreducible components of XksX_{{k}_{s}}. ∎

5.3. Zero-cycles of odd degree and rational points

Proposition 5.3.1.

Assume that kk is perfect. Let XX be a complete, geometrically connected variety of dimension one such that H1​(Xks,ℚl)=0H^{1}(X_{{k}_{s}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0. Assume that XX is the support of a snc divisor in some variety (§2.2). If XX supports a zero-cycle of odd degree, then X⁡(k)≠∅X(k)\neq\varnothing.

Proof.

Since dimX≤1\dim X\leq 1, the variety I=Sing⁡(X)I=\Sing(X) is finite. It follows from [Gro65, (6.7.4)] that Iks=Sing⁡(Xks)I_{{{k}_{s}}}=\Sing(X_{{{k}_{s}}}). Let X1,⋯,XmXX_{1},\cdots,X_{m_{X}} be the irreducible components of XksX_{{{k}_{s}}}. Since XksX_{{{k}_{s}}} is the support of a snc divisor in some variety (Lemma 2.2.1), each point of IksI_{{{k}_{s}}} belongs to exactly two XiX_{i}’s. Conversely any point of Xi∩XjX_{i}\cap X_{j} with i≠ji\neq j belongs to IksI_{{{k}_{s}}}. It follows that IksI_{{{k}_{s}}} is the disjoint union of the varieties underlying Xi∩XjX_{i}\cap X_{j} for i<ji<j, and that χ⁡(I)\chi(I) is the number of edges of ΓX\Gamma_{X}. By Lemma 5.3.2 below, it follows that

χ⁡(X)=∑iχ⁡(Xi)−∑i<jχ⁡(Xi∩Xj)=∑iχ⁡(Xi)−χ⁡(I)\chi(X)=\sum_{i}\chi(X_{i})-\sum_{i<j}\chi(X_{i}\cap X_{j})=\sum_{i}\chi(X_{i})-\chi(I)

From the assumption on H1​(Xks,ℚl)H^{1}(X_{{{k}_{s}}},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}) and by Lemma 5.1.2, we deduce that

(6) 1+mX=∑i=1mXχ⁡(Xi)−χ⁡(I).1+m_{X}=\sum_{i=1}^{m_{X}}\chi(X_{i})-\chi(I).

Since for each ii, the ks{{k}_{s}}-variety XiX_{i} is irreducible, we have

(7) χ⁡(Xi)=1−dimℚlH1​(Xi,ℚl)+1≤2.\chi(X_{i})=1-\dim_{{\mathbb{Q}_{l}}}H^{1}(X_{i},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})+1\leq 2.

From (6) and (7) we deduce that χ⁡(I)≤mX−1\chi(I)\leq m_{X}-1 with equality if and only if H1​(Xi,ℚl)=0H^{1}(X_{i},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0 for each ii. But ΓX\Gamma_{X} is a connected graph with mXm_{X} vertices and χ⁡(I)\chi(I) edges, hence χ⁡(I)≥mX−1\chi(I)\geq m_{X}-1. Thus χ⁡(I)=mX−1\chi(I)=m_{X}-1 and ΓX\Gamma_{X} is a tree. In addition, for each ii, the ks{{k}_{s}}-variety XiX_{i} is a smooth connected curve, whose genus is zero because H1​(Xi,ℚl)=0H^{1}(X_{i},{\mathbb{Q}_{l}})=0 by (7) (see e.g. [SGA73, IX, §4]). It follows that Xi≃ℙks1X_{i}\simeq\mathbb{P}^{1}_{{{k}_{s}}} for each ii. We conclude using Lemma 5.3.3 below. ∎

Lemma 5.3.2.

Let X1,⋯,XnX_{1},\cdots,X_{n} be closed subvarieties of XX such that Xi∩Xj∩Xl=∅X_{i}\cap X_{j}\cap X_{l}=\varnothing whenever i,j,li,j,l are pairwise distinct. If X=X1∪⋯∪XnX=X_{1}\cup\cdots\cup X_{n}, then

χ⁡(X)=∑iχ⁡(Xi)−∑i<jχ⁡(Xi∩Xj).\chi(X)=\sum_{i}\chi(X_{i})-\sum_{i<j}\chi(X_{i}\cap X_{j}).
Proof.

We proceed by induction on nn, the case n=0n=0 being clear. When n>0n>0, let Y=X1∪⋯∪Xn−1Y=X_{1}\cup\cdots\cup X_{n-1}. Then Y∩XnY\cap X_{n} is the disjoint union of the varieties Xi∩XnX_{i}\cap X_{n} for i<ni<n, and using the induction hypothesis,

χ⁡(X)\displaystyle\chi(X) =χ⁡(Xn)+χ⁡(Y)−χ⁡(Y∩Xn)\displaystyle=\chi(X_{n})+\chi(Y)-\chi(Y\cap X_{n})
=χ⁡(Xn)+∑i<nχ⁡(Xi)−∑i<j<nχ⁡(Xi∩Xj)−∑i<nχ⁡(Xi∩Xn)\displaystyle=\chi(X_{n})+\sum_{i<n}\chi(X_{i})-\sum_{i<j<n}\chi(X_{i}\cap X_{j})-\sum_{i<n}\chi(X_{i}\cap X_{n})
=∑iχ⁡(Xi)−∑i<jχ⁡(Xi∩Xj).∎\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\chi(X_{i})-\sum_{i<j}\chi(X_{i}\cap X_{j}).\qed
Lemma 5.3.3.

Assume that kk is perfect. Let XX be a complete kk-variety such that ΓX\Gamma_{X} is a tree and every irreducible component of the ks{{k}_{s}}-variety XksX_{{{k}_{s}}} is isomorphic to ℙks1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{{{k}_{s}}}. If XX supports a zero-cycle of odd degree, then X⁡(k)≠∅X(k)\neq\varnothing.

Proof.

We first reduce to the case when XX is irreducible by induction on the number of irreducible components of XX. Let us assume that XX is not irreducible, and let TT be the irreducible component of XX corresponding to the Gal⁡(ks/k)\Gal({{k}_{s}}/k)-orbit of a leaf in ΓX\Gamma_{X}. Note that the closure YY of X−TX-T in XX is non-empty. We may view the graphs ΓT\Gamma_{T} and ΓY\Gamma_{Y} as full subgraphs of ΓX\Gamma_{X}, compatibly with the Gal⁡(ks/k)\Gal({{k}_{s}}/k)-actions, and the set of vertices of ΓX\Gamma_{X} is the disjoint union of the set of vertices of ΓT\Gamma_{T} and ΓY\Gamma_{Y}. Since each vertex of ΓT\Gamma_{T} is a leaf of the tree ΓX\Gamma_{X}, it follows that ΓY\Gamma_{Y} is a tree (removing a leaf from a tree yields a tree or the empty graph). The irreducible components of YksY_{{{k}_{s}}}, being among those of XksX_{{{k}_{s}}}, are isomorphic to ℙks1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{{{k}_{s}}}.

Let PP be an irreducible component of TksT_{{{k}_{s}}}. We claim that in the graph ΓX\Gamma_{X} there is exactly one edge one of whose extremities is PP, and that the other extremity is an irreducible component of YksY_{{{k}_{s}}}. Since PP is a leaf in the tree ΓX\Gamma_{X}, there is at most one such edge. If there are none, then PP is the only vertex of ΓX\Gamma_{X}, hence P=XksP=X_{{{k}_{s}}} and XX is irreducible, a contradiction. Thus there is exactly one such edge, let QQ be its other extremity. If QQ is an irreducible component of TksT_{{{k}_{s}}}, it is a leaf of the tree ΓX\Gamma_{X}, and P,QP,Q are the only two vertices of ΓX\Gamma_{X}. Then T=XT=X is again irreducible, a contradiction. Therefore QQ is an irreducible component of YksY_{{{k}_{s}}}, which proves the claim.

From the claim we deduce that the irreducible components of TksT_{{{k}_{s}}} are pairwise disjoint (so that mT=μTm_{T}=\mu_{T}), and are in bijection with the points of the finite ks{{k}_{s}}-variety (T∩Y)ks(T\cap Y)_{{{k}_{s}}}. Thus μT∩Y=μT\mu_{T\cap Y}=\mu_{T}. If nTn_{T} is even, then nYn_{Y} must be odd. If nTn_{T} is odd, then so is μT\mu_{T} by Lemma 5.1.3, and thus also μT∩Y\mu_{T\cap Y}. The latter is the sum of the separable degrees of the residue fields of the points of the finite variety T∩YT\cap Y, which are in particular closed points of YY. Since kk is perfect, we deduce again that nYn_{Y} must be odd. Therefore in any case we may conclude the proof using the induction hypothesis for the variety YY.

Thus we may assume that XX is irreducible. Since the group Gal⁡(ks/k)\Gal({{k}_{s}}/k) acts transitively on the tree ΓX\Gamma_{X}, each of the vertices of ΓX\Gamma_{X} is a leaf. It follows that the graph ΓX\Gamma_{X} has no more than two vertices (and thus at most one edge). If XksX_{{{k}_{s}}} has two irreducible components, they meet in a single point (over ks{{k}_{s}}), which coincides with Sing⁡(Xks)=Sing⁡(X)ks\Sing(X_{{{k}_{s}}})=\Sing(X)_{{{k}_{s}}} [Gro65, (6.7.4)]. Since kk is perfect, it follows that Sing⁡(X)\Sing(X) is a rational point of XX. Otherwise, the variety XX is geometrically irreducible. Thus Xks≃ℙks1X_{{{k}_{s}}}\simeq\mathbb{P}^{1}_{{{k}_{s}}}, hence XX is a smooth conic over kk. Since XX supports a zero-cycle of odd degree, it must possess a rational point by Springer’s theorem. ∎

Remark 5.3.4.

It is not necessary to assume that XX is the support of a snc divisor in Proposition 5.3.1. An earlier version of this paper contained a proof of this more general statement, but as pointed out to me by Johannes Nicaise, Proposition 5.3.1 suffices for the proof of Theorem 4.1 and is substantially shorter to prove.
